Revised after game update: Where'd that well placed quit button go? My Thumbs Up is probably hanging out with it. . . . original: thumbs up only at a low price point, as a lite 15 min time fill. Otherwise it's a bit basic for billiards shooting with no spin control. It can be hard to predict exactly where your ball will wind up with no spin knowledge. As best as i can tell spin is determined by power. Full power is forward spin to chase a ball, half power is back spin for a little back spin. There is a rando power up to full stop if aimed +/-5% dead on. And due to the nature of needing to use full/much power for any shot that must travel enough distance and impart enough energy to the target ball. You just will chase it into the hole with regularity. While in reality you would still power hit, but ensure to provide back spin so you won't chase the target ball into the pocket. It is frustrating to know the only way to sink a ball is to sacrifice sink the cue ball too. Because of the fixed forward spin of the cue ball. So $6 max makes this an ok buy, if you're good for so lite a system.

It's okay. It was a decent distraction for a few hours but felt uninspired. All of the levels seem to be randomly generated. This means that you'll never be in a level and know what kind of shot to do. There's no opening "Break" and it's even possible for enemies to spawn huddled in corners with no pockets and barriers in the way. The spawning also feels very unbalanced. Sometimes the first level even spawns with a key (a second upgrade for the next round) which is the kind of thing you'd really want to be consistent. None of the upgrades (items) are exciting. Some of the upgrades only trigger once, usually on your first shot. Another chunk of the upgrades you can get give you a [i]chance[/i] of something happening, which is wonderfully boring. With a 20% chance of something happening you can't plan for it in advance, only hedge your bets. There doesn't seem to be any kind of rarity so none of the upgrades can do anything particularly powerful on their own. Where are things like multi-ball or a big size increase? Anything that makes me want to build around it. The art style is alright, but you really get no sense of how much the ball will spin around a pocket. There is only so much you can do with sprites but I think this game could do a lot more. Lastly, the name. It's really on the nose in a particularly bad way and it could have used an extra 5 minutes of workshopping.

Game is incredibly shallow and your choices border on inconsequential. It doesn't really matter what power-ups you purchase during your playthrough, because each session is so ridiculously short that by the time you get any sort of "build" going, the game is already over. The variability is so low that once you've played the game two or three times (which will happen in your first hour) you've pretty much seen everything it has to offer. If you're okay with dropping $5 for a fun little pool game that you'll play for an hour and then shelve permanently. Then it's an okay purchase, but don't be confused by the hype, this thing isn't a Balatro or Slay the Spire that you're going to sink dozens of hours into.

Rack and Slay is a worthy addition to your library, and a lot of addictive fun. Does it have lasting power? I'm not sure it does as much as the best roguelikes, but unlockable difficulty levels, an offering of many challenge modes, and an achievement set will keep you playing to see it all. I like how the shop system feels unique, and the item designs are quite fun. However, there may be a few too many items that generate gold or health, which can crowd out the neat effects that directly affect play. Critiques aside, this game is definitely worth the price, and it sparks joy in my pool-loving hands. Also, the creepy and contemplative music is not what I expected, in a good way! It makes coming back to the game relaxing and fun. The developer is very attentive and continues to provide updates and support based on player feedback.

Update: with the recent patch, there were a bunch of new stuff thrown into the mix. It feels more chaotic, than ever. You can't really chain nice anymore, because there are too many items in the pool. Honestly it should be a neutral review, maybe a 6/10. The idea is simple, but great. You play pool with special features. However I think the joy of freshness will run out rather quickly. My biggest problem is whit the design. As you "level up", you'll unluck new items, which gives you special powers. Normally leveling up means you're getting better, but not here. Higher level items doesn't equals better items. Even if so, you still aren't insured, that you'll see the item to pick. You can't manage them as a deck, so in the end you'll have a large amount of items in the mix. At the moment there are 112 items in the pool, but you'll be presented only with 3 options to choose from. The chance to get the items what are you hoping for is pretty slim. So as you progress, you're stratigic planning and options are turned more into RNG. You won't know what options you'll get. Adding salt to injury; I believe at least 1/3 of the items are really inferior, so you won't pick them at all, another 1/3 of the items are extremely situational and/or they'll work only well with other items, but again, you can't influence it to make it happen. Another issue is with the difficulty levels. I think under 10 feels easy, but above 15 feels really unfair, espacially if you've already unlocked everything. At this point you're left of the mercy of RNG Jesus. What is the layout? What type of enemies are on the map? Are you getting the right items in the right order? You can say it's a skill issue, but I think only the really good players can perform consistently on 20 difficulty level. So for me the sweet spot is somewhere above average. I don't like the options in which ways you can customize your experience. Lack of item control was already mentioned. To me 10 levels are the bare minimum to play, because it gives you the length to have a meaningful build in the end. I would like to have an option to have longer sessions with fewer items to pick up, so you can ramp up slower, but enjoy it a bit more. Endless mode was introduced, but it just let you play your extremely pumped up build to play on some additional levels. I don't see the point of the daily runs or the wild ones, except doing them for the achievements. I think the lack of variety kills the long term enjoyment. There isn't anything to come back after awhile. Maybe having different types of tables other than the rectangle may spice up the experience. My biggest fear is that the development will remain on the same course. It means there will be more items added to the roster or some new goofy game mode will be introduced, so you'll get only more from the same. The game is fun for a few hours. There is a demo, try it out! If you like it, then I think you'll get good value for your money.

The idea of a billiards RL is nice but this game fails to deliver. Cue sports are games of control and precision, whereas this game's mechanics only create disorder on the table, namely more explosions and more balls running around the table. These are also basically your two "build" options. It gets really boring really fast. You should note that [b] this game plays more like a minigolf/croquet [/b] than any kind of billiards or pool game as [b] you can't put spin on the ball. [/b] Furthermore, the [b] table is ridiculously slow [/b] and you have to build up your shot power stat each run to make even very basic shots from any kind of distance. Overall the game feels like an extremely uninspired stab at an interesting idea. Funnily enough I feel I might be okay with all the silliness of just blasting balls around if it was sold as a minigolf or croquet game, but even then I would probably feel the price is a bit high considering the variation in content. If you do end up getting this game, [b][u] do not expect a billiards game[/u][/b]: it's a vaguely billiards-themed ball smasher with underwhelming game design.

The reason I am giving this a bad review is because the game has a serious problem with agency, Most pool games have a way to control the cue ball. This game doesn't and it actually needs it MORE than other games as there are many holes and obstacles to avoid. So many turns you are forced to pot cue ball to make your shot. Many other turns you are stuck behind obstacles with no recourse. This made me lose interest in the game fast as it didn't feel like I have enough control of what goes on. TLDR: Cool idea that is ruined by lack of agency for the player.

"Do you like to get your balls sucked ... into strange pockets, with a weird gravitational pull?" -- nobody, ever. This is a weird one. Steam needs a "maybe". At first, Pool seems like an exciting idea for a rogue like. And I did enjoy a couple of hours with the game, during which I made it to difficulty 17 of 20. Some time during that, I got a queasy feeling. And no, it was not the Burrito I ate. There is simply too much going on. Don't get me wrong, there are rogue likes where this is a good thing. Watch everything light up in Balatro and only have a vague idea why that hand suddenly scores excessively big? Good thing. With Pool, turns out it's not. There are too many obstacles, too many explosions, too many weird deflections of balls that occasionally just seem like outright bugs - and cannons that fire at random. Towards the higher levels, this game can be outright infuriating, also for the strange design decision of keeping you "snookered" repeatedly. If I wanted to lose games for being repeatedly placed in impossible positions, I'd go back to playing 9-Ball at the pool hall with the local big shots. If you can play some pool, all this clutter adds too much ... fluff. And unpredictability, since you can't always judge pixel perfect whether an obstacle will be hit or not. And that's not even considering that at later levels, some tables are turned into effing pinball tables with reactive bumpers. Besides basic "rogue like economy strategy", there is ONE tool you have that determines the outcomes: position play. If you can play some pool, you know the concept. I mean, god knows mine sucks at the actual table, but it would help in this game, greatly. Thing is: your options to play position are entirely castrated here. There is no English (off-center queue ball play), so no varying of angles. There is no option to hit lower or higher, again cutting any option for varying angles with angled shots, and taking away any way to make the queue ball follow or being drawn back. Or at least I didn't even find any of these options. And to put icing on cake, or chalk on queue tip: No option to fine tune the stroke strength (no, this isn't an innuendo, and any others are pure coincidence!). You can't not strike the queue ball at least half a table no matter how fast you click the mouse with Diablo-honed speed clicking skills. In conclusion: This looks like a flashy pool table game seemingly designed by people of whom I wonder if they ever held a straight stick. Sometimes, maybe, less is more. Just like with some people, this game would have greatly benefited from a traditional layout of holes - not that random mess. And possibly a better pathing tool for the stroke, but definitely an addition to hit the queue ball off-center. I will give it the benefit of thumb skywards, alas, in reality, this is a meh++.

Do not buy this if you plan on playing it via a Steamdeck. I want to really like this game but I bought it thinking it'd be fun on the Steamdeck. Aiming is frustrating. Its cool, and I can forgive the glitchy physics but it's extremely frustrating on a controller (Steamdeck).

Great concept, fun if you like top-down billiard games. I am very picky about games so the following is only my opinion. Common roguelike features that I don't enjoy very much: - randomization makes some levels super easy and some near impossible - extreme power gap between helpful items and everything else Flaws (in my opinion) but still common in roguelikes: - random start pushes player to reset for better loadouts - permanent unlocks of bad items make it harder to reach good ones Then one design choice that I found extremely frustrating: - Playing well enough to have shots left makes you lose all remaining pickups
